Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi
(‘the wish-yielding gem of the four ends of life’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most voluminous and celebrated digests of ancient religious rites and observations is हेमाद्रि’s (13th cent. A.D.) चतुर्वर्ग-चिन्तामणि. हेमाद्रि who was a minister at the court of the Yādava king of Devagiri (modern Daulatabad in Maharashtra) might have composed this during A.

-70. According to the state-ments in the book, the author intended to treat the subject in five sections: vrata (religious observances), दान (gifts), tīrtha (pilgrimage), मोक्ष (emancipation) and परिशिष्ट (supplement). Since the sections dealing with tīrtha and मोक्ष are not available now, some scholars feel that हेमाद्रि could not complete his work according to his original intentions. The book is more popular in the Deccan and South India, and is considered as a standard work.

caturdhāma
(‘the four abodes of [God]’)
------------------------------------------
The four places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in the four corners of India, viz., बदरीनाथ in the north, Rāmeśvara in the south, Jagannātha पुरी in the east and द्वारका in the west—are the four dhāmas or abodes of God which every Hindu aspires to visit during his life time.
See under each for details.

Caturvyūhas
------------------------------------------
The भागवत or the Pāñcarātra religion, which preaches the cult of विष्णु-नारायण, puts forth the theory that the Supreme Lord विष्णु has four aspects of manifestation:
The पर or the supreme;
the Vyūha or the emanation;
the विभव or the इन्चर्नतिओन् and
the Arca or the icon.
Para is the Supreme as He is, in all His glory. विभव represents the incarnations. Arca is the descent of the Lord into the icon ceremonially installed and worshipped in the temples.
The व्यूहस् or the emanations are four in number. Hence the term Catur-व्यूहस्, also called चतुर्मूर्तिस्. They are: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध. According to Vaiṣṇava mythologies, while Śrī कृष्ण is वासुदेव, his brother बलराम is सङ्कर्षण. प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध are कृष्ण’s son and grandson respectively. Historically speaking, it is possible that these Yādava heroes were in course of time, apotheosised into these व्यूहस्. Symbologically, वासुदेव represents चित्त (mind-stuff), whereas सङ्कर्षण stands for अहङ्कार (egoity), प्रद्युम्न for बुद्धि (intellect) and अनिरुद्ध for मनस् (mind). They represent the cosmic psychological evolution.
Later on, these व्यूहस् were increased to as many as twenty-four. Icono-graphically, all these व्यूहस् are identical in appearance except for the arrangement of the four emblems—Śaṅkha, चक्र, गदा and पद्म.
The Pāñcarātra theology often adds another aspect of the manifestations, viz., the अन्तर्यामिन् (the indweller), which obviously, cannot be represented through icons.

caturthīkarman
(‘the rite on the fourth day’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu society has always consi-dered विवाह or मर्रिअगे as sacred, as a sacrament. The rites of मर्रिअगे breathe this spirit. The husband and the wife were expected to observe continence for three nights though sleeping together on the ground, with a दण्ड or staff between them. This was called ‘trirātravrata’ (‘the vow of three nights’). The मर्रिअगे was consummated on the fourth day—hence the name caturthīkarman—after appropriate rites. The smṛtis consider this as part of the rites of मर्रिअगे.
See also VIVĀHA.

Caturmukha
(‘the four-faced one’)
------------------------------------------
In Indian mythological accounts, ब्रह्मा the Creator, is called ‘Caturmukha’ since he has four faces, representing the four वेदस्. See BRAHMĀ for details.
In the works on temple architecture ‘caturmukha’ is the name given to a circular type of temple with four doors.

caturopāyās
(‘the four means [adopted by a king]’)
------------------------------------------
While dealing with other kings who may cause trouble to himself, either now or in future, a wise ruler should adopt the caturopāyas or four means judiciously. They are: sāma (reconciliation); दान (yielding something to appease him); bheda (bringing about a split in the enemy’s ranks) and दण्ड (going to war).

Catus-sana
(‘the four “Sanas” ’)
------------------------------------------
The four ‘mānasaputras’ or मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा, the Creator, are called ‘Catus-sanas’ since their names begin with the word ‘Sana’. They are: सनक, Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta and Sanandana. They are in the state of eternal boyhood.
Once they went to वैकुण्ठ, the abode of विष्णु but were denied admittance by the gatekeepers, जय and विजय. Hence they were cursed by the sages to be born on earth as demons. जय and विजय, consequently, took birth as हिरण्याक्ष and हिरण्यकशिपु, रावण and कुम्भकर्ण, and Siśupāla and दन्तवक्र.
The sage Sanatkumāra taught the greatness of विष्णु to Vṛtra (the demon enemy of इन्द्र) and spiritual wisdom to नारद, another great sage. Sanatsujāta taught spiritual truths to धृतराष्ट्र, the blind king and ड़थेर् of the Kauravas like दुर्योधन. सनक is said to be an eternal companion of Lord विष्णु. Sanandana is accepted as an ancient teacher of Sāṅkhya, more ancient than even कपिल.

caturviṁśati-mūrti
(‘twentyfour forms’)
------------------------------------------
In Vaiṣṇavite rituals, very often, 24 names of विष्णु like Keśava, नारायण and वासुदेव are used. All these names refer to the same deity and give his attributes from different standpoints. Iconographical works have devised a simple method by which these 24 aspects of विष्णु can be shown, just by altering the positions of the four well-known appurtenances viz., शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). For instance, if they are held—in that order—in the right upper and lower hands, and, left upper and lower hands, the image is that of वामन. If, on the other hand, the right upper and lower hands hold the गदा and the शङ्ख, and, the left upper and lower hands hold the चक्र and पद्म, it is the image of वासुदेव.
The 24 names are: Keśava, नारायण, Mādhava, Govinda, विष्णु, Madhusūdana, त्रिविक्रम, वामन, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न, अनिरुद्ध, Adhokṣaja, पुरुषोत्तम, Nṛsiṁha, Acyuta, Upendra, Janārdana, Hari and कृष्ण.
See VIṢṆU for symbology.

caturvarga
(‘the group of four’)
------------------------------------------
The four ‘puruṣārthas’ or ends of life to be sought after by all human beings are called ‘caturvarga,’ ‘the group of four’. They are धर्म (righteousness), अर्थ (wealth), काम (pleasures of the flesh) and मोक्ष (release from transmigratory existence). Sometimes, the first three are called ‘trivarga’ (‘group of three’) and मोक्ष as ‘apavarga’ (‘that which is beyond the group’).
See PURUṢĀRTHAS for details.

cāturmāsya
(‘four-monthly’)
------------------------------------------
Certain वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् belonging to the ‘iṣṭi’ group (See IṢṬI.) are known as ‘cāturmāsya’ since these sacrifices have to be repeated every four months. They are: वैश्वदेव, वरुणप्रघास, साकमेध and शुनासीरीय. (See under the respective titles for details.) Each is called a ‘parvan’ or a part of the Cāturmāsyas. They were performed respectively on the full-मोओन् days of Phālguna or चैत्र (February—April), आषाढ (July), Kārttika (November) and on the fifth full-मोओन् from the day on which the साकमेध is performed. Obviously these are the beginnings of the spring, monsoon and autumn seasons. The Maruts were the most prominent deities receiving offerings in all of them with the set of gods peculiar to each. The attainment of हेअवेन् was the promised fruit. These sacrifices could be performed either throughout one’s life or for one year only.
The four months of the rainy season are also called ‘cāturmāsya’. A ‘vrata’ or a religious observance, has been prescribed for these months for those who are interested, by the smṛtis and धर्म-śāstras. It begins with a सङ्कल्प or resolve on the 11th or the 12th day of the bright half of आषाढ (July), or on the full-मोओन् day. During these four months, the person under the vow, should desist from consuming some specified edibles like vegetables, curds and milk, and give up some luxuries such as cot. It is to be concluded on the Utthāna-द्वादशी day (12th day of the bright half of Kārttika which generally comes in November). Many rewards, both here and hereafter, have been promised to those that observe this vrata. It is open to women also.
The saṁnyāsins (monks) also have a चातुर्मास्य. During the days when the saṁnyāsins were mendicants, realizing the difficulty of moving about during the rainy season, it was made obligatory for them to spend the four or even two months of the rainy season by camping in a suitable place. Their vrata or vow begins on the व्यास-pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day in आषाढ), with a ceremonial worship of God, the sage वेदव्यास and one’s gurus (preceptors). (Hence the day is also called ‘Guru-pūrṇimā’.) During these days they can live in the congenial company of other मोन्क्स्, study the scriptures, practise their personal spiritual disciplines and also preach to the householder devotees that may approach them.

caturviṁśati-tattva
(‘24 cosmic principles’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Sāṅkhya system of philosophy it is प्रकृति or प्रधान comprising the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्, that is the originator of this world. It evolves in stages into 23 fundamental principles—itself being the 24th—by the permutation and combination of which the whole world is created. They are: प्रकृति (Mother Nature), महत् (‘the great’, the intellect), अहङ्कार (egoism), मनस् (mind), five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of sense), five कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action), five तन्मात्रस् (subtle elements) and five bhūtas (gross elements).
See SĀṄKHYA-DARŚANA for details.

Caturvedasvāmī
(‘master of the four वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. Their language is archaic. Their ideas are often unintelligible. Hence a bhāṣya or a commentary is necessary to understand them.
Out of the several commentators on the ऋग्वेद, some like सायण, are well-known. Among the lesser known ones is Caturvedasvāmin. He lived at the end of the 15th cent. A.D. Sūryapaṇḍita, who wrote a commentary on the Līlāvatī of भास्कर (12th cent. A.D.) was his disciple.
His explanations of ṛks have been considered as rather odd since he often connects them to the epic personalities like the Pāṇḍavas.

caturthavisarga
(‘giving up the fourth’)
------------------------------------------
Honouring the dead ancestors through appropriate rituals is a pheno-menon common to many cultures. Such a ceremony among the Hindus is called ‘śrāddha’. Riceballs called ‘piṇḍas’ are offered to the ancestors with suitable mantras during these ceremonies.
In one of these śrāddhas called ‘pārvaṇaśrāddha,’ the offerings are made to the dead ancestors up to three generations (father, grandfather and great-grandfather) only, omitting the fourth and beyond (visarga = omitting). This is called ‘caturthavisarga’.
See also PĀRVAṆA-ŚRĀDDHA and ŚRĀDDHA.

caturguṇa
(‘the four qualities’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu scriptures, by and large, have given a very high status to the king, even calling him as ‘pratyakṣa-devatā’ (‘visible deity’). It was his primary duty and responsibility to protect the lives, properties, honour and religion of his subjects at any cost. Whatever he did for discharging this, was considered धर्म or righteousness, as long as he had no selfish or impure motives.
For this, he was advised to employ four kinds of ‘upāyas’ or means which were technically called ‘guṇas.’ They are: sāma (conciliation), दान (concessions, favours and gifts), bheda (dissensions) and दण्ड (conflict and war).
The enemies of the State could be internal or external, the former being considered as the more dangerous. The king was advised to make use of the daṇḍopāya as the last resort. He was to try for conciliation through sweet words, concessions, favours and gifts. If these did not have the desired effect, then he should secretly try to bring about dissensions among the enemies and trouble-makers through spies of proven loyalty. दण्ड or war was to be the last resort.
Both मनु and कौटिल्य have dealt with this subject in detail.
